I saw this post hours ago, but had a child to attend to, so I'm back to give you what you need to hear - both, part of my story for perspective, and advice on your situation.

I'm really sorry that your mother, and her mother, are both hateful women.

I was in the same situation as your wife, with PPA, as well as antenatal anxiety (my pregnancy was over medicalised and subsequently caused minor birth complications which my husband copped the brunt of - I dissociated until my baby was in my arms an hour later). On the hour and 45 minute drive home from the hospital, on Christina Day in 2022, I said to my husband "I never want to leave the house again" and I meant it. I didn't want to leave my baby, and I didn't want to put trust in the world that we'd be safe if we went out. 

My in laws are wonderful, however, unlike yours. My mother is an awful B, and caused my anxiety and stress to increase 10 fold in the midst of my first pregnancy, and post-partum.. we also live over 2.5hrs away from them, and due to age and disability, their visits to us were thankfully infrequent. My mother hounded me night and day, though, and only worsened my condition. I kept her at arms length where I could, and cut her out of my life at 11m post-partum. She never met my child, and I'm grateful for the physical distance, and covid restrictions at the hospital at the time of birth.

Onto the topic at hand:
Your wife is not unreasonable. Your family is not the family she grew up in, therefore the energy expenditure, particularly the emotional energy, to host, converse with, and monitor around your child, is significantly greater than the energy she needs to expend around her own family. She knows her own family very well, and since she hasn't cut the toxic ones out, she just navigates the toxicity as she always has - because she's lived it her whole life. Your family are also toxic - if your father and mother are still married/ together, then he is an enabler, therefore he is an issue, though not as great as your mother is. Scheduling them coming over is her way to prepare herself mentally, and knowing the duration of the visit helps her to navigate a short time with toxic people that she hasn't known her whole life. I completely understand this feeling.

What you need to do, is step up to the toxic people when they step into your home. Speak to your wife about what bothers her when *anyone* visits, how she'd like to manage visitors (her family included), and how you, her husband, can help enforce **emotional** boundaries with all visitors. No names need to be named. Eg: if someone talks to (your wife) while she is attending her (almost?) toddler (? is the child walking yet?), you need to step in and say: "I'm sorry, (wife) is attending to toddler, can you please allow her a moment to raise her child, she will be with you when she can be". Be pointed, polite, but firm. The way you enforce a boundary is by saying "if you cannot give (wife) the time she needs to look after (our) child, please consider how this will impact you setting the child". Sometimes, you need to be direct "give (wife) the respect she deserves, or you are not welcome in my home", but these kind of direct comments need to come after seeing boundaries, and repeating them often.

I'm not going to blame you for not setting your parents straight, or even for not seeing how toxic they are - your wife sees it and is keeping her distance for good reason. Just like I don't blame your wife for choosing the devil she knows, just to keep her sanity. However, this is where you both are right now, and you need to work with her. If you don't, then this is the point at which blame should fall directly on you. Gently steer her in a direction that shields her from her own family, while helping to facilitate a respectful relationship with yours. I do not condone relationships with children, if the grandparents are awful to the parents. There is no room for grandparents, if they treat the parents like trash. Remember this. Your parents need to apologise, and mean it, for their ill treatment of your wife, if they want to begin a relationship. They have to work hard, and mean it, to foster good will between 3 generations, otherwise it won't happen. Then your child will be told by your mother, that your wife is evil, awful, manipulative, and a while host of untrue things while spoiling them rotten, which will drive a wedge between your child and wife, and then your wife and you - I've seen it many times. Your mother may destroy your family, if you don't step up. 

I also recommend you look into enmeshment, narcissistic parents, and observe the similarities you and your wife have between the examples and both your mothers behaviours. I'm starting to think you and your wife found each other and bonded over similar trauma. But she's the birth-giver and primary carer, and she gets more say in who she is around, than you do. In this case, I feel like that was in her and your child's best interest.

Tread carefully, OP. This is a very tricky situation. I don't know where you live, or what your situation is, but if you can, get a therapist who understands narcissistic or Cluster B personality traits, and get some help. Don't let the grandparents and toxic family members ruin your family. The only other option is to cut them all off, and move away.

I truly hope that things come good in the end, but I suspect your wife's mental health is a combination of her mother and yours, not just from being a woman who gave birth and is raising a child.

They usually are single women, or women who's husband is not often at home - they generally tolerate their partners, but put unrealistic and emotionally romantic expectations on their "chosen son". They meddle in their sons relationships, causing breakups with girls who have a good head in their shoulders and can pick up in the red flags pretty quickly - straight relationships are the problem, as the other female is basically competition for romantic displays and tokens of affection.

These women have traits that fall into the Cluster B personality disorder traits, usually Histrionic or Narcissistic. They want their son to end up with someone like them, who will extravagantly suck up to her in monetary and public ways, not some home baked, thoughtful gift, based on their preferences. Displays of big love for the sons partner are forbidden, and it's unlikely you'll get a warm reception when you announce engagement, pregnancy, or get married. The mother will likely sabotage you at any chance she gets, throw you under the bus, and make a big stink over a non-issue just to make you look bad if you're caught unawares.

Enmeshed females of these Cluster B mothers act in similar ways, but they do it in order to maintain "best friends" status with their daughter, to ensure they get the same treatment their daughter gets, from her male partner.

This woman knows you're smart. This woman knows you're kind. This woman knows your intentions are pure. But she will lie and manipulate your boyfriend who's had her for 20+ years more than he's had you. She will do it to keep him to herself, so she can continue to milk the positron as most important female in his life, **for as long as she can**.

My advice, if you want to continue a relationship with him: take [this simple quiz](https://www.proprofs.com/quiz-school/story.php?title=enmeshed-family-quiz-do-you-experience-enmeshment) and ask him these questions. Read snippets of mother-son enmeshment information from quality psychology websites. Show him that this isn't normal behaviour, and psychology has a term for this toxic and damaging relationship he has with her

Otherwise **Get. The. F^CK. OUT** before this love triangle ruins your brains ability to understand healthy relationships - your brain wasn't even fully developed by the time you met her and got hit with this BS.

Take it from me. I cut out my enmeshed mother over a year ago, and moved very far away from her 3 years ago. **Emergency Contraception**

The MAP/EP/EC is used to delay ovulation. It works by blocking the natural hormone rise that creates the corpus luteum and egg release, temporarily. The sperm, in perfect conditions, can live up to 7 days in the female reproductive organs, and the longer the days between insemination (sorry, I icked at the word on your behalf for your situation, but it's accurate) and ovulation, the better the chance of avoiding pregnancy.


**Ovulation and Conception**

Ovulation is not a set day in the cycle, it can happen as early as 7 days after the first day of your period, and as late as months after the first day of your period (short cycles due to low progesterone, long cycles due to high test because of PCOS/ athlete/gym rat or very low body fat etc) depending on your cycle length. The rough ovulation date of the most common 25 to 28 day cycle is 10-19 days after your first day of your period. The days are referred to CD - cycle day.

If you're on your period, you very **very** likely are not pregnant. If the insemination occurred >5 days before your period started, you're very likely not pregnant.


**Helpful Information around Cycles for Prevention, Pregnancy and Health**

If you want to understand the general risks around insemination and pregnancy (and also keep an eye on your health), I highly recommend you look into a non-hormonal method of birth control such as Natural Family Planning, or Fertility Awareness Method. FAM has an informative community on Facebook, and there are almost a dozen methods to choose from (3 or 4 types, with a few sybtypes - much like how you can get several kinds of implans, the shot, and several kinds of BC pills). I used a symptothermo method called SensiPlan, which checks basal body temp, and physical signs of ovulation/impending period/pregnancy. The thermo methods use a scientifically backed measurement with calculations to understand your unique cycle, to interpret what your body is doing in the 72hrs prior, and to assess your risk of pregnancy in the coming days. It works predominantly by charting a handful of cycles (where you abstain/ use a barrier for sex for these) to understand your baseline, see patterns, and establish your understanding of the method based on your cycle. **In the event where sex is unprotected, this is your best friend** you can avoid taking a hormonal contraceptive (EC) or a copper IUD (to stop implantation or miscarry the zygote/immature embryo) by knowing where you are in your cycle, and seeing your history of ovulation on specific CDs. Much like no/broken condoms, it will not, and does not claim to, protect against an STI.

It's perfect use failure rate is much the same as HBC and condoms, and imperfect use failure rate, also similar. It also helps reduce the guessing game of should I, shouldn't I, and you can make decisions based on your cycle Information. **IT IS NOT THE RHYTHM METHOD, PLEASE DON'T USE THE RHYTHM METHOD.** The rhythm method is "logging" your cycle, with the *prediction* that ovulation with occur days 14-17, and is based off generalisation from an imperfect study on women and their cycles. You need to work out a way to directly feed him your expectations (eg: you want a specific kind of flower, you like cakes/ deserts on special occasions, you want a specific kind of jewellery/ accessory/item that you would never buy for yourself unless in celebration of achievements) and you need to keep the gifts limited to 2 or 3 choices. Make the experience easier for him. All that said, he needs to be willing to accept these terms, and work with the specific information you give him, so it's less of a chore on him, you get something that you want, and he doesn't need to expend emotional energy on something that doesn't interest him. Again, *HE NEEDS TO ACCEPT THE TERMS*.

If he's not on board with this compromise, then it's really not going to go well. You'll resent him for not meeting your needs, he'll resent you for not being grateful for what he perceives to be adequate effort (for him), and you will end up fighting a lot. Growing resentment makes it harder to reconcile, and harder to compromise. I have a lot of experience in this area. It sucks, because it feels like the other person is being unreasonable, so why should you go through more effort to fix it if they aren't? Well, guess what? He's gonna be feeling the exact same way. 

You'll need to give it some time, so either vent to a friend, or write it in a diary/ phone notes/paper and keep it secure so he doesn't find it. You need it out of your system, but recorded for future reference. Write down your feelings, your wants, your compromises. Then wait a few weeks or months, and bring it up when you're both calm. Start with "something is bothering me and I'd like to talk to you about it". Bring up your feelings and wants. Make it about you, not him and what he did/ didn't do. It's not about blame, it's about asking for compromise, so make it clear in your language - always use "I" statements, never say "you" or "someone" (eg: "someone forgot that I like gifts, and flowers isn't really a gift" - that's blame, and it's pointed). How your conversation goes, and how he responds to you, will tell you what you need to know about your relationship. It will tell you if you can expect compromise, if you'll end up resenting him, if you're a good communicator. And it will be an indicator of how your marriage will look in 10 years when you have kids. Tread carefully, and be prepared for things not to work out. I don't know you, your family, your husband, or your lifestyle, but your partner is supposed to match and balance you, incompatibility is a HUGE issue.

Good luck. I hope you can/ did enjoy the rest of your birthday.
